blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define a mixed economic system and place it between the market and command systems.

blocks.heading: Sharing the decisions
blocks.text: A mixed economic system is an economic system in which the what, how and for whom questions are answered partly by market forces and partly by government. Private firms, owned by private owners, decide what to produce in response to prices and profits. Government decides a further share of allocation through its budget, its public services and the firms it owns. Neither side runs the whole economy: the market answers for much of daily buying and selling, and the state answers for the services and investments it judges the market handles badly.

blocks.heading: Between market and command
blocks.text: A market economic system leaves allocation to private owners responding to prices. A command system places allocation in the hands of a central authority that sets targets and owns the productive assets. A mixed system combines elements of the two: it keeps private property, prices and profit-seeking firms, while government directs a share of resources itself and steps in where it judges a market outcome to be failing. The balance differs from country to country; one mixed economy may lean towards the market, another towards the state.

blocks.heading: Two mixed economies in practice
blocks.text: Namibia allocates everyday goods through markets: a Katutura bakery decides each morning how many loaves to bake by reading yesterday's sales, minibus owners set fares that fill their seats, and shops in Oshakati stock what their customers ask for. Beside that market half stands the state half: government pays for state schools, state hospitals and the freight railway out of the budget, corrects prices it judges harmful, and owns a share of the country's firms. Germany mixes the same way from the other end: world-scale private firms trade internationally while the state runs the schools, much of the railway and wide rules for banks. What makes both economies mixed is the shared feature - prices answer the allocation questions the state leaves open, and government answers the rest.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The market system this topic builds on is taught in topic 2.9, and the failures of a market system that pull government in - needs the market leaves unmet, costs pushed onto bystanders - are taught in topic 2.10. The wider jobs of government belong to topic 4.1.
